summary: The Ludington harbor light since 1870, now a 1924 steel tower at the end of the north breakwater, city-owned and run by volunteers; closed for the 2026 season.

access.note: Half-mile walk down the north pier from Stearns Park; tower climbs by ticket when open; closed for the 2026 season, reopening 18 May 2027 (Lakeshore Keepers).

facts.agency: City of Ludington; operated by Lakeshore Keepers since 2006

events.note: Wooden pierhead beacon on the south pier, fixed red, fifth-order lens
Thirty-foot wooden tower, painted white
Pierhead crib and light washed away in a heavy gale, December 1876
Tower rebuilt in the spring of 1877
Tower moved 140 feet to the end of the extended pier
Pierhead light moved 750 feet lakeward to the third crib from the end after the south pier extension
754-foot elevated walk built on the south pier
Ten-inch steam whistle in operation 31 January 1895
Beacon moved close to the signal house; covered way built; whistle moved
Keeper's dwelling completed (contract 1900)
Fog-signal building and light tower moved 200 feet to the end of the south pier; skeletal tower erected behind (LighthouseFriends)
Timber breakwaters completed
Pere Marquette Car Ferry No. 18 struck the north breakwater in fog on 10 February 1922, destroying a section of timber breakwater
Steel tower on the north breakwater; light and fog signal commissioned 30 December 1924
Fourth-order lens, diaphone fog signal worked from shore
Radiobeacon established at the station
Fourth-order lens replaced by a modern beacon on 17 October 1995; lens loaned to White Pine Village
National Register of Historic Places, NRIS 05000982
National Park Service transferred the light to the City of Ludington in May 2006
Fourth-order lens restored, then moved to the Port of Ludington Maritime Museum (opened 2017)

corrections.proposed: steel tower built 1924, 57 ft (17.4 m) above mean high water
corrections.why: The USLHS record gives the tower established 1924 and a height of 57 ft above mean high water; LighthouseFriends dates the steel tower to 1924. The 1871 date is not supported by any source read; the 1870 wooden pierhead tower is the first.

corrections.proposed: City of Ludington (owner); Lakeshore Keepers (operator since 2006)
corrections.why: LighthouseFriends says the City of Ludington owns the light since 2006; Lakeshore Keepers says it has operated the light since 2006 with the city.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1871 'built' date for the steel tower conflicts with the 1924 tower date. The Board's 1891-1892 report says a light had been kept on the south pier since 1870, and LighthouseFriends dates the steel tower and its commissioning to 1924, consistent with the USLHS tower date.

notes_for_editor: Tower material: the USLHS place record says steel and reinforced concrete on a wooden crib filled with rock and concrete; LighthouseFriends says a steel-plate tower; the story says steel. Name of the operator: LighthouseFriends names the Sable Points Lighthouse Keepers Association; Lakeshore Keepers' own page says it has operated the light since 2006 with the city. The story gives both. Keeper's name: LighthouseFriends prints Girard in its 1872 account and Gerard in its keeper list; the roster has Gerard. The 1890 Oceana County history was not read (quod.lib.umich.edu returned 403); the 1872 Souvenir rescue is cited to LighthouseFriends as quoting that history. LighthouseFriends-only facts (not checked against a primary text): the 1876 washout, the 1880 move, the 1904 move, the 1907 breakwater authorization, the 1914 completion, the 1924 date of 30 December, the 1927 radiobeacon, the 1995 lens change, the 2016 restoration. Dwelling: the contract (1900) and completion (1901) are from the Board reports; LighthouseFriends gives construction from May 1900. Whistle hours: the 1895 report gives 306 hours for the first, part-year season; the 1896-97 report gives 607 hours for the year. The Board's 1894 request for the keeper's dwelling ($4,500) appears in the 1894 volume (annualreportlig01statgoog, scan 336) and is repeated in the 1895 volume, which is the one cited. The Life-Saving Service's Station No. 7 at Ludington (1880) is not used; it is a separate station record. The NRHP form is not digitised (NPGallery PDF placeholder). The listing date is from the NPGallery asset record. Visiting hours: LighthouseFriends gives summer hours from an undated note; Lakeshore Keepers says the light is closed for 2026 and reopens 18 May 2027. Check before publishing hours. Light List Iso G 6s is the record's character; the Light List's height and range columns were not used because their layout is ambiguous in the text extract. Fact-check 2026-10-22: the 1894 request for a $4,500 keeper's dwelling is cited to the 1894 Board report (scan 480), which the story now footnotes as 14; the 1895 estimates repeat it. LighthouseFriends says the dwelling was begun in May 1900 and completed later that year; the 1901 Board report records it as completed; the story gives both without choosing. Operator: LighthouseFriends names the Sable Points Lighthouse Keepers Association (city agreement, 2006); Lakeshore Keepers says it has operated the light since 2006 in partnership with the city. The story gives both. USLHS lists 'Open to Public: No' for this station; LighthouseFriends and Lakeshore Keepers say it is open, so the story states the USLHS entry. The Girard/Gerard spelling is LighthouseFriends' own (account vs keeper list). The 1890 Oceana County history was not read directly; the story attributes the account to LighthouseFriends. Melvin N. Nelson appears in the roster (1956 onward, no end date). He is named only as USLHS prints him, in the roster; the story prose does not name him. A human should confirm before the roster is published that this listing is acceptable under the living-person rule (DESIGN and STORY_GUIDE).
